questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was important for me that the courses at the university sounded interesting and that it was a country I hadn’t visited before.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I really only had good experiences with McGill University and Montreal in general. It's quite different from Copenhagen but not too overwhelming at the same time. The city is just amazing.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Before starting classes I had a walk around campus to find my class rooms since campus is quite big. I know they also provide guided tours for new students, but I did not sign up. A lot of the needed information is also easily found on the McGill website and through E-mail.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I don't recall getting any assistance upon arrival. A week before the Semester starts the student advisor of the science faculty had arranged a meet-up for all international exchange student and she also advised every exchange student to to set up a private meeting with her. I found this very helpfull as she made sure the courses I was signed up for matched my background at UCPH. She is also very willing to answer any questions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: In my experience finding housing was very easy. I had some friends who went on exchange in Montreal a year before me and they helped me reach out to their old landlord and got an apartment 20 min walk from campus. Personally I really enjoyed living off-campus. When you live on-campus or in residence you have to join a mandatory meal-plan which was quite expensive. At my stay most of the exchange students living in campus housing lived at Solin hall, which is kind of far from campus and city center (you have to take metro or bike to campus) but I really appreciated being able to walk to campus. It was also cheaper in my case to live in an apartment with 2 roomies than living on campus.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is most likely cheaper than living on campus. It is a student city so many people rent rooms or apartments. I did not meet any exchange students experiencing difficulty in finding off-campus housing.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I found it very expensive and far away from the city center but it is a very easy way to find new friends. I visited the residence Solin Hall which seemed very nice with a big living room and kitchen and two bathrooms but I also heard people living at dorms in University Street had lower standards.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Once you understood the registration process it was very easy, maybe a bit old school. I don't think they have updated the website for many years.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I found the whole process very stressful. Firstly, I found it difficult to find a list with all the courses available in the fall semester. Secondly, the registration for courses opens later for exchange students, which meant that many of the courses I originally wanted where already full. For some of the courses you can get waitlisted, but not for all courses. At the end i managed to get into all the courses I originally wanted. In the beginning of the semester they have a add/drop period where many people change courses, so if you can't register at first just wait till the add/drop period. 

I also wanted to join a course that had pre-requisites. Here I had to E-mail the professor until I could register.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The visual schedule builder found on Minerva was a very big help in seeing how many spots that are available in the different courses and to make a schedule with no overlaps.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Stay calm if the course you want is full. Know that all the courses you look up beforehand might not be available.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took courses in physiology, biology and french. 

FRSL 302 Listening Comp & Oral Exp 1 (french): This is the easiest course I had at McGill.  I really don't think you can fail the course. I did most of my homework and all assignments with moderate/low effort and still managed to get an A. 

BIOL 575 Human Biochemical Genetics: Compared to KU and considering this is a master course, this was also a very easy class. You get most of you grade points through presentations and everyone got a 100%/A. I had passed the course before even taking my final exam. 

PHGY 314 Integrative neuroscience: This class was definitely the hardest course I had at McGill. The curriculum is very big and the exam is a multiple choice closed-book exam. Still though I would say that the level was maybe a bit lower than at UCPH. 

PHGY 488 Stem cell biology: This course was very similar to the level at UCPH in terms of content.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In my physiology and my biology courses the teaching style was very similar with lectures. In most of my courses there was no reading material except of the lecture slides which was very nice. In my french course we had a lot of oral assignments and discussions and a lot of homework which was different.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
FRSL 302 Listening Comp & Oral Exp 1 (french)
BIOL 575 Human Biochemical Genetics
PHGY 314 Integrative neuroscience
PHGY 488 Stem cell biology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
French: I would recommend taking a french course if you'd like to be able to speak a bit with the Quebec people. It was a fun class and many exchange students take it, so it's a good way of making friends. Many first year students take it, so people were a bit young. Depending on your french skills you get placed on a course matching your level which is very nice. I was in FRSL 302. 

If you are interested in stem cells I cannot recommend PHGY 488 Stem cell biology enough. This was the best course I had at McGill. You meet people from the field, not many universities provide stem cell courses, and the professors were very nice.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not any that I can think of.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were more expensive than anticipated but dining out is cheaper than in Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are student clubs for everything at McGill. They also have sport events like football and basket. They honestly have everything.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend McGill Book Club, Knitting club, Nordic culture club, seeing a football game, joining an a capella group (or going to a capella concert) or McGill Choir society.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Visit the Insectarium (small museum about insects), Biodome, The Montreal science center, Redpath museum on campus

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It is very easy. People are more open and talkative than in Copenhagen which makes it very easy to make friends.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I found this quite hard since most of the students aren't local. Like finding actual Canadian people was not easy haha. But I would say by joining a club or a sports team it's easy to make friends. At my stay we also had a big whatsapp group with all the exchange students where we planned different activities. In some of my classes people were also willing to socialize.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I once went to the doctor and he only spoke french which was a bit of a challenge but it worked out in the end.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How open and welcoming the people of Montreal are. People are just very kind and nice.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Don't be scared if a course with a high number (like 500-level courses) are going to be too hard - they are not
Join a club, it is fun
DON'T join frosh if it is offered to you, it was a waste of money and time

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Enjoy, it is going to be so much fun

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Making new friends was the most rewarding part and getting to live in another country was really a good experience

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The workload is a bit more intense throughout the course at McGill compared to UCPH where you only have a final exam.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
